standard.title: Select tools for content creation
standard.description: Select and use appropriate digital tools effectively to create, locate and communicate content, applying common conventions
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can use the core features of common digital tools to create, locate and communicate content, following agreed conventions (AC9TDI4P06). They have used digital tools with provided guidance. They have not yet selected tools themselves — the shift is from using a nominated tool to choosing the appropriate one for a task.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students select appropriate digital tools for creating, locating and communicating content, plan achievable steps and timeframes, apply common conventions, and judge the appropriateness of content for the audience.

nodes.label: Planning and selecting tools for a task
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can plan achievable steps and timeframes for a task and identify which digital tools are needed at each step
nodes.minimum_width: For a given task, list the steps needed and identify at least one digital tool for each step
nodes.typical_width: Create a plan with achievable steps and realistic timeframes for producing a digital solution; identify the specific tools needed for each stage (e.g. word processor for report, spreadsheet for data, presentation tool for communication); explain why each tool suits its step
wider: Plan a school recycling report that requires multiple tools at different stages — search tools for data, a spreadsheet for analysis, a word processor for writing, and a presentation tool for sharing — identifying where the output of one tool becomes the input of the next
Develop a plan for a collaborative spreadsheet to cost a school celebration — identifying which features (shared editing, formulas, tagging) make it the appropriate tool for this task

response_modes.reason: Tool selection is a reasoning task — students must work backwards from what the task requires to which tool's features match those requirements. Scaffolding the selection reasoning (what does this step produce? → what tool produces that format?) prevents students defaulting to the one tool they know.

success_criteria: Lists steps for the task with realistic timeframes
Identifies at least one appropriate digital tool for each step with a reason

nodes.label: Locating content effectively
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can locate relevant content using search engines and within documents by refining queries
nodes.minimum_width: Perform a search, evaluate the results, and refine the query at least once to improve accuracy
nodes.typical_width: Locate content through search engines using effective query strategies — reviewing results, refining terms, using required search syntax; locate content within documents using find/search features; distinguish between more and less reliable sources
wider: Compare search results from two different queries on the same topic and explain why the refinement improved accuracy — identifying what the changed terms added or removed from the results
Verify AI-generated content about a local topic against an authoritative source — demonstrating the difference between locating information and accepting generated text as factually accurate

response_modes.reason: Students typically use the first search results they find and do not evaluate or refine. Seeing how the same question yields different quality results with different query strategies — and how AI-generated content can appear authoritative while being incorrect — builds the habit of verification rather than acceptance.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The AI-generated content verification direction (from the elaboration) is rich — it directly addresses a contemporary and age-appropriate challenge: students are encountering AI-generated text in search results and need to evaluate it critically.
success_criteria: Refines a search query at least once and explains what the refinement improved
Identifies at least one reason why a source may or may not be reliable

nodes.label: Judging appropriateness for audience and context
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can judge whether content they have created or located is appropriate for the intended audience and purpose
nodes.minimum_width: Review a piece of content (created or located) and explain whether it is appropriate for the intended audience — identifying at least one reason it is or is not suitable
nodes.typical_width: Apply multiple appropriateness criteria to content — is the tone right for the audience? Is the content accurate? Is the format suitable? Revise content where it does not meet these criteria
wider: Judge the tone of AI-generated text against the intended audience — deciding whether autocomplete or generative text is too formal, too informal, or inaccurate for the specific context and rewriting accordingly
Compare the same content created at different stages of an iterative process — explaining how teacher or peer feedback changed what was appropriate in subsequent versions

response_modes.reason: Students treat content as finished once produced. The judgement reasoning scaffold — audience / tone / accuracy / format / verdict — makes appropriateness a multi-dimensional check rather than a gut feel, and teaches revision as a response to evidence rather than preference.

success_criteria: Identifies the intended audience for the content
Gives at least one criterion-based reason for whether the content is appropriate for that audience
